sources.locator: §3.4 (printed pp. 34–41), §§4.2–4.3 (printed pp. 44–52), §§4.9–4.13 (printed pp. 70–99) and §§9.1–9.4 (printed pp. 360–391); the table of contents and the named sections were read, exercises excluded

contents.name: §3.4 The classical construction: groups of words (free words, normal forms, concatenation)
§§4.2–4.3 Imposing relations on groups and presentations of groups via the free object and the quotient universal property
§4.9 Tensor products of abelian groups via the universal bilinear property
§4.10 Monoids, free monoids and the word construction for monoids
§4.12 Rings: free commutative rings are polynomial rings, and the monoid-ring construction R[M]
§4.13 Coproducts and tensor products of rings
§§9.1–9.3 Varieties of algebras, generating algebras from below, and terms and left universal constructions (free algebras and their universal property)
§9.4 Identities and varieties: equational theories and variety characterisations
contents.reason: The pair uses only the universal property of the free algebra and of a quotient by relations; the variety-classification theorems are not needed.

sources.title: Keith Conrad, Tensor products (University of Connecticut expository notes, 60 pp.)
sources.locator: §§1–7, printed pp. 1–60; the full note was extracted and inspected, with §§1–3 and §§5–6 read for the constructions and proofs and §4 and §7 checked for scope

contents.name: §1 Introduction: general tensors are finite R-linear combinations of elementary tensors; bilinear maps as the motivating universal problem
§§2–3 Bilinear maps and the construction of M⊗N: Theorem 3.2 (existence), Theorem 3.3 (spanning-set computation), Theorem 3.5 (zero tensors), Example 3.6 (Q⊗ZA=0)
§4 Examples: Theorem 4.1 (Z/aZ⊗Z/bZ), Theorem 4.5 ((R/I)⊗M≅M/IM), Theorem 4.9 (product bases of free modules), Theorem 4.14 (tensor powers of free modules)
§§5.1–5.4 symmetry, associativity and distributivity isomorphisms and the multilinear re-description of iterated tensors
§§5.6–5.11 Hom–tensor adjunction, the map M^∨⊗N→Hom(M,N), its finite-free isomorphism and the examples of failure in infinite dimension
§§5.16–5.19 testing a linear map on elementary tensors and non-injectivity phenomena on tensor products
§6 Base extension: Theorems 6.4 and 6.7, Examples 6.8–6.9 (S⊗RR[X]≅S[X]), Theorem 6.11 (direct sums), Theorems 6.21–6.22 (fraction-field base change)
§6 torsion and rank computations over fraction fields (Theorems 4.27, 6.13–6.16, Corollary 4.28)
contents.reason: Base change to the universal fraction field is consumed by the generic Hecke semisimplicity page; this page's A8 constructs the fraction fields but does not prove these torsion/rank formulas. This destination is a future unselected proof home; no completion of its additional claims is promised by this run.

contents.name: §7 Tensors in physics: the coordinate-transformation (component) definition of tensors
contents.reason: The page defines tensors by multilinearity and the universal property; the component-transformation presentation is a physical convention that no item on this pair consumes.

§§13.1.5–13.1.6 Remarks: S⁻¹R as an explicit presented R-algebra and Z[X,X⁻¹] corepresenting the unit functor
§13.3 The tensor product: Proposition 13.3.4 (existence), Propositions 13.3.6–13.3.7 (symmetry, unit), Propositions 13.3.9–13.3.10 (adjoint property, commutation with colimits)
§§13.3.13–13.3.20 base change adjunction and tensor products of algebras as coproducts
§§13.4.1–13.4.3 right exactness of the tensor product and the failure of exactness
§§13.4.4–13.4.17 flatness, projectivity and finitely presented base change
contents.reason: Flatness and projectivity are not assumed anywhere on this pair: the quotient base-change step uses right exactness alone, and the injection lemma uses field complements instead of flatness.
